claims.summary: Near the 900 CE horizon, Ibn Rustah describes Rūs groups raiding by ship, taking people identified as Saqaliba captive, transporting them to Khazar and Volga Bulgar markets, and selling them. Specialist source-critical work independently situates extensive ninth-century Viking captive-taking and a broader northern/eastern European slave-trade system around the same period. This supports bounded external slave-trade-network participation, not one Viking polity, one homogeneous people, or territorial slavery across connected regions.

claims.summary: Private and government slavery are well attested under the Western Han, but the evidence does not support treating slave labour as a dominant industrial or agricultural system. claims.summary: Stable-isotope, archaeological and contextual analysis of the Zhengzhou Shang City skull ditch concludes that the individuals were most likely prisoners of war captured during early Shang military expansion. The atlas records recurrent coercive captive-taking at this bounded site/context while explicitly not translating the remains into proof of slave status. The separate slavery interpretation remains disputed.
